Joe Rogan turns to what first drew Robert Bigelow to UFOs in a segment from his show. Bigelow is the aerospace rich man who funded UFO hunts and built space gear. His love for the topic has shaped the field for years.

Rogan works through the tales told of Bigelow's start: a family sighting, a bought ranch of high strangeness, and deals with the state. He asks why a hard-nosed builder would pour cash into ghosts and craft. The segment is short and rich with lore. Listeners get a quick life sketch of a key funder. The library holds the file as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-ORB4j8Z1W1A:
Rogan watches the Pfizer chief's 2019 comments about pills with sensors in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. The clip shows the CEO describing, with pride, a pill that can signal when a patient has swallowed it. Rogan's reaction is the episode.

He turns the remarks over slowly, asking who such tracking serves and where consent fits in. The talk widens into drug firms, digital monitoring, and the thin line between care and control. The segment is a small artifact of pandemic-era distrust, built around a few sentences of corporate candor that landed very differently than intended.
uslaw-usc-t2-s141a:
Section 141a of Title 2 of the United States Code, in the chapter on the Library of Congress, moves responsibility for the Library's security systems. The duty to design, install, and maintain systems that protect the physical security of the Library's buildings and grounds passes from the Architect of the Capitol to the Capitol Police Board. The work is done under the direction of two committees: House Oversight and Senate Rules and Administration.

The transfer is made without regard to the general procurement statute named in the text. One safeguard is kept for the Architect. Any change to a structural, mechanical, or architectural feature of the Library's buildings and grounds that a security system requires may be carried out only with the Architect of the Capitol's approval.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1801a:
Section 1801a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the appointment and term of service of the Architect of the Capitol. It sits in Chapter 28 of Title 2, on that office, in the general subchapter. The version here is current through Public Law 119-134.

The Architect is to be appointed without regard to political leaning, and solely on fitness to do the duties of the office. Appointment is by majority vote of a congressional commission named in the section. Its members include the Speaker of the House, the majority leader of the Senate, and the minority leaders of both Houses. They also include the chair and ranking minority member of the House Appropriations Committee, and their counterparts for the Senate committee, as the text goes on to list.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1881a:
Section 1881a of Title 2 of the United States Code provides Capitol flown flags for the families of fallen heroes. It sits in the flags part of the Architect of the Capitol chapter. At the ask of a close family member, the family's Representative or Senator may give the family such a flag.

The dead must have been a firefighter, law officer, rescue squad or ambulance crew member, or public safety officer who died in the line of duty. The flag is given at no cost to the family. A signed paper goes with the flag. It is signed by the Speaker and the member, or by the President pro tempore and the Senator, as the case may be. It carries a word of sympathy from the House or the Senate.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1901a:
Section 1901a of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the Capitol Police Board. It sits in Chapter 29, on the Capitol Police, in a general part of the chapter. The end of the Board is set out first. The Board is to watch over and to back the Capitol Police in its work. It is also to push joint work between the Capitol Police and the two Sergeants at Arms, in their work as keepers of the law, and with Congress.

In line with that end, the Board is to set the wide aims and marks of its main work. Those aims are to raise the skill and the worth of what the Board does. A second clause deals with the make-up of the Board. The text shown is cut off at the head of that clause.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1921a:
Section 1921a of Title 2 of the United States Code gives the Capitol Police Board and the Chief of the Capitol Police sole power over rates of pay. It sits in Chapter 29 of Title 2, on the Capitol Police, in the part on pay and other personnel matters. The version here is current through Public Law 119-134.

The key clause is short: the Board and the Chief shall have the sole and exclusive authority to set rates and amounts for members of the Capitol Police. The items listed start with the rate of basic pay, including the rate of basic pay on appointment. The list goes on to premium pay and to pay for specialty assignments. No other office shares that pay-setting power under this section.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1a: Section 1a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers how a senator's election is certified. It sits in the opening chapter of the title, on the election of senators and representatives. The chief executive of the state from which a senator has been chosen must certify the election. The certificate goes under the seal of the state to the President of the Senate of the United States.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2131a:
Section 2131a of Title 2 of the United States Code sets eligibility for placement of statues in National Statuary Hall. It sits in Chapter 30 of Title 2, in the preservation subchapter, current through Public Law 119-134. The rule is a waiting period tied to the person honoured.

No statue of any individual may be placed in National Statuary Hall until ten years have passed from the date of that person's death. The bar does not apply to two classes of statue. One is the statue obtained and placed under the Act named in the section. The other is any statue given by a State under section 2131 of the title, or any replacement statue given by a State under section 2132.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2171a:
Section 2171a of Title 2 of the United States Code allows charging stations for private cars in Library of Congress parking areas, at no net cost to the government. Funds appropriated to the Architect of the Capitol under the Capitol Power Plant heading may be used to build, run, and maintain the stations. The work is done on a reimbursable basis. A covered employee is a Library employee, or any other person allowed to park in the areas.

The Architect may use one or more vendors, on commission terms, to run the stations. The aim is that users' payments cover the costs. The section thus lets Library staff charge electric cars at work without a net charge to public funds.
uslaw-usc-t2-s281a:
Section 281a of Title 2 of the United States Code states the purpose of the House Office of Legislative Counsel. That office helps turn policy ideas into bill text. Its mission is stated in terms of language, not politics.

The office exists to advise and assist the House, its committees, and its Members. The goal is a clear, faithful, and coherent expression of legislative policies. The office must keep strict impartiality on the policy issues themselves. Those issues are for the House to decide, not its drafters. The office shall not push for the adoption or rejection of any bill. One exception is named: when the Speaker or a committee duly asks it to comment, as the text goes on to say. The section makes the drafter a servant of every side and an advocate of none.
uslaw-usc-t2-s661a:
Section 661a of Title 2 of the United States Code sets out definitions for its subchapter on credit reform. It sits in Chapter 17A of that title, on congressional budget matters. The first term defined is direct loan. A direct loan is a payment of funds by the government to a borrower outside the federal sphere. The payment is made under a contract that calls for the funds to be paid back, with or without interest.

The term is stated to take in more than that core case. It covers the purchase of, or a share in, a loan made by another lender. It also covers finance deals that put off payment for more than ninety days. The sale of a government asset on credit is named as a case of that kind. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s901a:
Section 901a of Title 2 enforces a budget goal through automatic reductions. Discretionary appropriations and direct spending accounts are reduced in line with a set calculation. The Office of Management and Budget computes the deficit reduction required by the section for each of the fiscal years 2013 through 2021.

The calculation starts from a fixed sum stated in the text. From it, the reduction achieved by enactment of a joint committee bill is subtracted. The difference is then reduced by eighteen percent, to account for debt service. The result is divided by nine, for the nine years in view. A further fixed reduction applies for fiscal year 2013. The section then turns to the allocation of the cuts to budget functions. It sits in Chapter 20 of Title 2, on emergency powers to eliminate budget deficits. The hosted Code is current through Public Law 119-134.
